THE STORY BEHIND THE NUMBERS

Where generations had suffered, a new beginning became possible.

On the grounds of a brick kiln in Pakistan, a painful story of inherited debt became a remarkable testimony of faith, dignity and compassionate action. This is the story of the mothers who asked for one daughter to be helped—and of a church that chose to stand beside eighteen.

01 / THE ENCOUNTER

A mother’s plea from the brick kiln

In January 2024, a pastoral visit to a congregation in Sheikhupura District brought the Church of Pentecost Pakistan face to face with the hardships of families caught in a cycle of inherited debt.

Sixteen women, most of them widows, approached church leaders. According to their accounts, brickmaking work brought in approximately US$10 a day, with nearly half deducted toward outstanding debts. Their deepest concern was the future of their daughters.

With wedding expenses beyond their reach, one mother proposed that the church write down all sixteen daughters’ names and draw one at random. Even if only one girl received help, she said, the other mothers would rejoice.

02 / A FAITH-FILLED RESPONSE

Not one daughter. All sixteen.

Rev. Dr. Jamil Nasir and the church leadership could not ignore the question: what would happen to the fifteen mothers whose daughters were not selected? Instead of drawing one name, they committed to helping all sixteen.

As word spread, two additional families with similar needs were welcomed. What began as a request for assistance for one young woman grew into a promise to help eighteen daughters start a different chapter.

The decision launched months of prayer, planning, pastoral support and coordination with the families and brick-kiln owner.

03 / PREPARATION

Practical compassion: more than a ceremony

The undertaking required arranging eighteen marriages, addressing debt pressures, preparing the venue, welcoming relatives and helping the couples establish households.

The church organized essential furnishings and equipment: beds, sofas, tables, cabinets, crockery and other necessities. These items represented more than gifts. They were intended to give each couple a foundation without new wedding-related borrowing.

04 / DECEMBER 6, 2024

A place of hardship became a place of celebration

The event took place on December 6, 2024, on the same brick-kiln grounds where families had worked for years. Brick production was suspended for the occasion, and the site became a gathering place for brides, grooms, relatives, pastors and friends.

The Church of Pentecost Pakistan reports that more than 2,000 people attended. Food, hospitality, seating and the wedding facilities were arranged so families who had endured financial hardship could celebrate with dignity.

The message was visible to everyone present: those who have lived under poverty and debt deserve honour, opportunity, community and hope.

05 / THE WEDDINGS

Eighteen couples. One unforgettable day.

Eighteen brides and grooms were welcomed to the platform. Church ministers guided the marriage ceremonies, read Scripture, prayed for couples and celebrated with the gathered community.

It was not merely a public event. It was a powerful act of solidarity with families who once believed even a modest wedding would be impossible.

06 / A NEW BEGINNING

Restoring dignity and equipping new households

The commitment did not end after the vows. Home furnishings and basic household goods were provided to the newly married couples, reducing the immediate financial pressure of building a home.

The initiative reached thirty-six families connected to the eighteen marriages, according to the church’s report. It offered these households encouragement and practical support in their journey away from generational debt bondage.

As the church continues serving brick-kiln communities, its wider mission remains clear: to proclaim the Gospel through words and acts of tangible compassion.

“Let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
1 John 3:18 · KJV
